subject: Chemistry

source.publisher: Federal Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education

outcomes.text: Use Al-Ghazali's burning cotton example to discuss limits of inductive reasoning in chemistry.
Explain that shells and subshells contain degenerate orbitals of equal energy.
Compare protons, neutrons and electrons by relative charge and mass.
Recognise that atomic number and proton number mean the same thing.
Recognise that mass number and nucleon number mean the same thing.
Describe how proton, neutron and electron beams of equal speed behave in an electric field.
Work out numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions from the given numbers and charge.
Explain how atomic and ionic radius change across a period and down a group.
Write electronic configurations of elements and ions, as shells or subshells, and link valence electrons to properties.
Define shell, subshell, orbital, principal quantum number and ground state.
Relate quantum numbers to how electrons are distributed.
State how many orbitals s, p, d and f subshells have and how many electrons each holds.
Use the aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule to write configurations.
Give the order of increasing subshell energy for s, p, d and f.
Describe configurations by electrons per shell, subshell and orbital.
Explain configurations using electron energy and electron-electron repulsion.
Determine configurations of atoms and ions from proton or electron number and charge.
Show why electronic configuration matters in designing materials for electronics, such as silicon.
Describe the shapes of s, p and d orbitals.
Describe a free radical as a species with unpaired electrons.
Explain that ionisation energy comes from nucleus-outer electron attraction.
Use ionisation energy to explain trends across periods and down groups.
Account for the jumps in successive ionisation energies of an element.
Explain how nuclear charge, radius, shielding and spin-pair repulsion affect ionisation energy.
Deduce electronic configuration from successive ionisation energy data.
Deduce an element's place in the periodic table from successive ionisation energies.
Explain how a mass spectrometer gives relative atomic mass from isotope composition.
Calculate relative atomic mass from isotope abundances, including from mass spectra.
Define electronegativity as an atom's power to attract bonding electrons.
Explain what affects electronegativity: nuclear charge, radius and shielding.
Explain electronegativity trends across a period and down a group.
Use Pauling electronegativity differences to predict ionic or covalent bonding.
Describe covalent bonding using sp, sp2 and sp3 hybrid orbitals.
Compare reactivity of covalent molecules using bond energy and bond length.
Describe molecular shapes and bond angles using VSEPR, including sketches.
Predict shapes and bond angles of molecules and ions.
Explain hybridisation and its types.
Explain valence bond theory.
Explain how VSEPR shapes help predict drug interactions in the body.
Explain the main features of molecular orbital theory.
Explain why oxygen is paramagnetic using molecular orbital theory.
Calculate bond order for N2, O2, F2 and He.
Describe the van der Waals forces: London dispersion, permanent dipole and hydrogen bonding.
Describe hydrogen bonding in N-H, O-H and H-F molecules such as ammonia, water and HF.
Use hydrogen bonding to explain the unusual properties of ice and water.
Use electronegativity to explain bond polarity and molecular dipole moments.
State that ionic, covalent and metallic bonds are generally stronger than intermolecular forces.
Recognise expanded octets in polyatomic ions such as sulfate and nitrate.
Analyse dative bond formation in CO, ozone and the H3O+ ion.
Read balanced equations in moles, particles, masses and gas volumes at STP.
Explain limiting reagents.
Calculate maximum product and leftover excess reagent.
Calculate theoretical, actual and percentage yield.
State the molar volume of a gas at STP.
Solve mole-volume problems using the molar volume at STP.
Find the molar mass of a gas from its density at STP.
Convert between mass, volume and particle number using moles.
Calculate reactant and product quantities in reactions using stoichiometry.
Explain why stoichiometry matters for making and dosing medicines.
Explain why photovoltaic cells are a sustainable energy source, using the photovoltaic principle.
Describe liquid properties using kinetic molecular theory.
Describe the types of intermolecular forces.
Explain the strength and uses of dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding and London forces.
Describe evaporation, vapour pressure, boiling point, viscosity and surface tension of liquids.
Use hydrogen bonding to explain water's high surface tension, specific heat, heat of vaporisation and boiling point.
Define molar heat of fusion and molar heat of vaporisation.
Describe how heats of fusion and vaporisation affect particles in matter.
Outline why heat of fusion matters for glaciers and polar ice.
Describe gas properties: compressibility, expandability and pressure.
Describe liquid crystals and their everyday uses.
Tell liquid crystals apart from pure liquids and crystalline solids.
Describe solid properties using kinetic molecular theory.
Tell amorphous from crystalline solids.
Describe crystalline solid properties: shape, melting point, cleavage planes, habit and growth.
Describe exothermic and endothermic enthalpy changes and their signs.
Interpret reaction pathway diagrams showing enthalpy change and activation energy.
Define standard conditions and the enthalpies of reaction, formation, combustion and neutralisation.
Explain that energy transfer comes from breaking and making bonds.
Calculate reaction enthalpy change from bond energies.
Describe why some bond energies are exact and others approximate.
Calculate enthalpy changes from experimental data using q = mcDT.
Define enthalpy of atomisation, lattice energy and first electron affinity.
Use enthalpy of atomisation, lattice energy and electron affinity terms.
Explain what affects the electron affinity of elements.
Construct Born-Haber cycles for ionic solids.
Do calculations with Born-Haber cycles.
Explain how ionic charge and radius affect lattice energy size.
Apply enthalpy change to hydration and solution.
Build an energy cycle linking enthalpy of solution, lattice energy and hydration.
Calculate with energy cycles.
Explain how ionic charge and radius affect enthalpy of hydration.
Define entropy as the number of ways particles can be arranged.
Explain entropy change signs for state changes, temperature change and changes in gas molecule count.
Calculate reaction entropy change from standard entropies.
Explain heat as a form of energy.
Explain how temperature relates to particle kinetic energy.
State that total energy is conserved in chemical reactions.
Explain standard conditions and standard states for energy measurements.
Explain Hess's Law.
Use Hess's Law to find enthalpy change for multi-step reactions.
Relate bond formation energy to bond breaking energy.

subtopics.title: Gibbs free energy and food energy

outcomes.text: Explain Gibbs free energy.
Use Gibbs free energy to solve problems.
Outline how enthalpy change relates to the calorie content of food.

subtopics.title: Rate of reaction and activation energy

outcomes.text: Explain reaction rate and the rate constant.
Calculate a reaction rate from experimental data.
Explain activation energy and its role in reactions.
Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain how temperature affects rate.
Explain how catalysts speed reactions by lowering activation energy.
Interpret reaction pathway diagrams with and without a catalyst.
Explain how Gibbs free energy change relates to the equilibrium constant.
Use rate equations, orders of reaction and rate constants.
Calculate a rate constant from initial rates and half-life data.
Suggest a mechanism consistent with a rate equation and rate-determining step.
Describe how temperature changes the rate constant and reaction rate.
Describe reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium as equal forward and reverse rates.
Define dynamic equilibrium between two physical states.
State the conditions for equilibrium and how to recognise it.
Describe the microscopic events at equilibrium with examples.
Write the Kc expression for a homogeneous reaction.
Relate different equilibrium constants such as Kc and Kp.
Write equilibrium expressions using concentration, partial pressure or moles.
Tell microscopic from macroscopic events in a system.
Propose microscopic events that explain observed macroscopic behaviour at equilibrium.
Decide whether Kc rises or falls with temperature from the reaction equation.
State and apply Le Chatelier's Principle to concentration, pressure, temperature and catalyst changes.
Explain industrial uses of Le Chatelier's Principle in the Haber and Contact processes.
Discuss using equilibria to maximise yield and cut waste in industry.
Use hydrolysis to explain why some salt solutions are acidic or basic.
Define a conjugate acid-base pair.
Identify conjugate acid-base pairs in reactions.
Apply conjugate acid and base ideas to salt hydrolysis.
Define pH, Ka, pKa and Kw and use them in calculations.
Calculate [H+] and pH for strong and weak acids and alkalis.
Distinguish Lewis acids (accept lone pairs) from Lewis bases (donate them).
Calculate the pH of buffer solutions.
Understand and apply the solubility product, Ksp.
Write Ksp expressions.
Calculate Ksp from concentrations and the reverse.
Apply the common ion effect to explain solubility changes.
Do Ksp calculations involving a common ion.
Explain why aqueous solutions of some salts are acidic or basic through hydrolysis.
Calculate [H3O+] from Ka and concentration of a weak acid.
Calculate ion concentrations of slightly soluble salts.
Carry out acid-base titrations to find molarity and strength.
Choose suitable indicators for acid-alkali titrations.
Explain how elements are arranged in the periodic table.
Explain that the table has four blocks tied to the subshell being filled.
Recognise that the period number is the outer occupied energy level.
State that the energy level and valence electron count follow from an element's position.
Locate metals, nonmetals and metalloids in the table.
Explain periodic trends in radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.
Link metallic and non-metallic character trends to valence electrons.
Work out electron configuration from table position and the reverse.
Write equations for Na and Mg reacting with oxygen, chlorine and water.
Explain oxidation numbers of oxides and chlorides from valence electrons.
Describe reactions of acidic and basic oxides with water and the resulting pH.
Explain acid-base and amphoteric behaviour of oxides and hydroxides, with equations.
Explain reactions of chlorides with water and the resulting pH, with equations.
Explain periodic trends in terms of bonding and electronegativity.
Suggest bonding types in oxides and chlorides from their properties.
Predict properties of an element in a group using periodicity.
Deduce identity and table position of unknown elements from their properties.
Explain trends in ionisation energy and electron affinity for Groups 1 and 17.
Describe the colours and volatility trend of chlorine, bromine and iodine.
Describe the trend in halogen molecule bond strength.
Explain halogen volatility using instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces.
Describe halogens' relative reactivity as oxidising agents.
Describe halogen reactions with hydrogen and their relative reactivity.
Describe and explain thermal stability of hydrogen halides using bond strength.
Describe halide ions' relative reactivity as reducing agents.
Explain halide ion reactions with aqueous silver ions and concentrated sulfuric acid.
Describe halide reactions with silver ions then aqueous ammonia.
Interpret chlorine's reaction with cold and hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.
Explain chlorine in water purification through HOCl and ClO-.
Explain nitrogen's low reactivity from its strong, nonpolar triple bond.
Describe ammonia's basicity using Bronsted-Lowry theory.
Identify the ammonium ion's structure and how it forms.
Describe displacing ammonia from ammonium salts with bases.
Describe nitrogen oxides, their sources and catalytic removal from exhaust.
Explain NO and NO2 in photochemical smog and PAN formation.
Tell nitrification from denitrification.
Explain sulfur's low reactivity using its bonding.
Describe sulfur's oxidation states and their relative stability.
Describe sulfuric acid's properties, production and industrial uses.
Describe sulfur reactions such as combustion and oxidation.
Explain uses of sulfur compounds in fertilisers, gunpowder, rubber, dyes, drugs and fragrances.
Identify the composition and properties of the atmosphere.
Describe the factors that affect air quality.
Describe sources and effects of natural and human air pollutants.
Describe methods for measuring and monitoring air quality.
Describe human impact on the atmosphere, including fossil fuel burning and deforestation.
Identify atmospheric reactions such as smog and acid rain formation.
Identify laws and rules that protect air quality.
Analyse air quality data and trends.
Explain the link between air quality and human health.
Evaluate health risks from air pollution.
Explain technologies that cut air pollution, such as emission control and renewables.
Design experiments to test ideas about air quality.
Identify global air pollution problems such as global warming and the greenhouse effect.
Analyse economic, social and political issues of air quality management.
Identify types of water pollution, such as point source and heavy metals.
Identify common water pollutants such as oil and pesticides.
Explain sources and effects of water pollution on people.
Explain water treatment methods such as filtration and purification.
Explain laws that cover water pollution and conservation.
Evaluate human impact on water from agriculture and industry.
Explain strategies for protecting and conserving water.
Explain water's chemical properties and how they relate to water quality.
Recognise hydrocarbons as compounds of only carbon and hydrogen.
Recognise alkanes as simple hydrocarbons with no functional group.
Recognise that the functional group decides physical and chemical properties.
Interpret general, structural, displayed and skeletal formulae.
Use systematic naming for simple aliphatic molecules with functional groups.
Deduce molecular or empirical formula from a structural formula.
Describe organic terms: homologous series, saturation, fission, free radical, nucleophile, electrophile and reaction types.
Define catenation and explain why it matters in organic chemistry.
Describe terms for organic mechanisms: free-radical substitution, electrophilic addition, nucleophilic substitution and addition.
Draw mechanisms with curly arrows for substitution, addition and elimination.
Use the term planar for arrangements of atoms in organic molecules.
Describe structural isomerism: chain, positional, functional group, metamerism and tautomerism.
Classify hydrocarbons as aliphatic or aromatic.
Name alkanes and cycloalkanes.
Explain shapes of alkanes and cycloalkanes, using ethane and cyclopropane.
Explain why alkanes do not react with polar reagents.
Define homolytic and heterolytic fission, and free radical initiation, propagation and termination.
Describe free radical substitution in alkanes using methane and ethane.
Identify organic redox reactions.
Explain how alkenes are named.
Explain the shape of ethene from its structure and bonding.
Describe the structure and reactivity of alkenes using ethene.
Explain isomerism terms with suitable examples.
Explain making ethene by dehydrating alcohols or dehydrohalogenating halogenoalkanes.
Describe ethene reactions: hydrogenation, hydrohalogenation, hydration, halogenation, epoxidation, ozonolysis and polymerisation.
Explain conjugation in alkenes with alternating double bonds.
Use IUPAC names for alkenes.
Describe electrophilic addition in alkenes with bromine/ethene and HBr/propene.
Explain alkyl group inductive effects on carbocation stability and Markovnikov addition.
Classify halogenoalkanes and explain how structure affects reactivity.
Predict products of simple halogenoalkane syntheses from alkanes, alkenes and alcohols.
Describe nucleophilic substitution of halogenoalkanes with NaOH, KCN, NH3 and silver nitrate.
Describe elimination from bromoethane with NaOH in ethanol to give an alkene.
State how alcohols are made, with reagents and conditions, and describe alcohol combustion.
Describe converting alcohols to halogenoalkanes with HX, KBr/acid, PCl3, PCl5 or SOCl2.
Describe hydroxy compounds reacting with sodium.
Describe oxidising alcohols with acidified dichromate or permanganate to carbonyls and acids.
Describe dehydrating alcohols to alkenes with a heated catalyst or concentrated acid.
Describe ester formation from alcohols and carboxylic acids with an acid catalyst.
Classify alcohols as primary, secondary and tertiary, including multi-alcohol examples.
State distinguishing tests such as the orange-to-green dichromate change.
Deduce a CH3CH(OH)- group from the alkaline iodine yellow precipitate test.
Explain why alcohols are more acidic than water.
State how aldehydes and ketones are made by oxidising alcohols.
Describe reducing carbonyls to alcohols and reacting them with HCN to give hydroxynitriles.
Describe the nucleophilic addition mechanism of HCN with aldehydes and ketones.
Describe using 2,4-DNPH to detect carbonyl compounds.
Tell aldehyde from ketone using Fehling's and Tollens' tests.
Deduce a CH3CO- group in a carbonyl from the alkaline iodine test.
Recall how carboxylic acids are made by oxidation and hydrolysis.
Describe carboxylic acid reactions with metals, alkalis, carbonates, alcohols and LiAlH4.
Recall how esters are made from an alcohol and carboxylic acid.
Describe ester hydrolysis with dilute acid and dilute alkali.
Define primary and secondary amines and explain their basicity and reactivity.
Tell primary from secondary amines by structure and chemistry.
Describe preparing amines by nucleophilic substitution and reducing nitro compounds.
Explain properties of phenylamine and azo compounds, including dye uses.
Explain organic synthesis and functional group interconversion.
Identify functional groups using characteristic reactions.
Predict properties and reactions from the functional groups present.
Devise multi-step synthetic routes.
Analyse a synthetic route for reaction types, reagents and by-products.
Explain retrosynthesis and its use in organic synthesis.
Tell petrochemicals from chemicals derived from them.
Identify raw materials for the petrochemical industry.
Explain fractional distillation and refining of petroleum and its fractions.
Describe the building block processes of petrochemical technology.
List major petrochemicals and why they matter today.
Distinguish energy density from specific energy and explain energy transfer efficiency.
Explain how fossil fuels form, their properties, uses and importance.
Explain nuclear fusion and fission and the importance of nuclear energy.
Explain how solar energy works and why it is a key renewable source.
Explain the environmental impact of energy use, global warming and sustainable alternatives.
Weigh advantages and disadvantages of energy sources to make informed choices.
Identify chemical hazards in a lab experiment.
Check equipment works safely before an experiment.
Keep the workspace uncrowded and safe.
Keep a safe distance from others handling apparatus.
Identify possible physical, chemical, biological and safety harms in an experiment.
Ask the lab instructor for help with unfamiliar apparatus.
Identify the proper disposal route for chemical waste.
Set up apparatus from written or diagram instructions.
Use apparatus to collect enough data.
Make careful observations of colour, solubility and quantity.
Measure with pipettes, burettes, cylinders and thermometers.
Decide how many tests or observations to make.
Identify when repeat readings are appropriate.
Repeat readings as needed, including when an anomaly is suspected.
Identify when confirmatory tests are needed and what they are.
Choose reagents to tell given ions apart.
Carry out procedures with simple apparatus even when the method is unfamiliar.
Describe an acid-base titration with burette, pipette and indicator.
Describe finding a titration endpoint with an indicator.
Describe tests for carbonate, halide, nitrate, sulfate and sulfite anions.
Describe tests with sodium hydroxide and ammonia to identify common cations.
Present data in one table with headings and units, and record raw readings to consistent precision.
Show working and key reasoning steps in calculations.
Use correct significant figures for calculated quantities.
Draw a results table before taking readings and fill it in.
Choose a clear method to present data.
Plot variables on labelled axes with suitable scales.
Draw straight lines or smooth best-fit curves on graphs.
Describe patterns and trends in tables and graphs.
Summarise the key points of a set of observations.
Find the gradient of a straight-line graph and extrapolate it.
Draw conclusions from experiments and test them against a hypothesis.

topics.title: Suggest Improvements Based on Validity, Reliability and Safety

outcomes.text: Draw conclusions from observations, data and calculated values.
Explain data, observations and conclusions scientifically.
Analyse the inherent errors of measuring devices.
Describe systematic errors.
Identify the biggest sources of error in an experiment.
State uncertainty as an absolute or percentage error.
Analyse limits of experimental design and propose accuracy improvements.
Evaluate the validity of the methods used.
Explain improvements or extensions to the methods used.
Apply scientific language effectively.
Credit the work of others and sources used.
Suggest ways to extend the investigation to a new question.
Suggest greener alternative chemicals for experiments.

warnings: unit "Domain A" (grade 11) has a single outcome
